title: After the last page
hook: the Tanakh closes, and Jewish history goes on
carry: the pages ran out; the handing-on didn't

segments.voice: Yesterday, trope: the small marks that tell a reader how to chant. Your line was where the verse breathes is where its thought divides. Today, what comes after the last page.

Close a Tanakh and look at the last printed page. A few days ago we heard its final words: Cyrus's call to the exiles, let him go up. Then white space. And yet the people in that book did not stop on that page. Somebody went up. Somebody rebuilt a wall, planted a vineyard, argued with a neighbor, married, buried a parent, taught a child to read the very scroll that had just run out of pages. A book can end. A people keeps waking up the next morning. Today we step off the last page into the long stretch of Jewish life the Bible itself never narrates.
screen: `THE LAST PRINTED PAGE.` → `THEN WHITE SPACE.` → `A PEOPLE WAKES UP THE NEXT DAY.`

segments.voice: The Talmud, in tractate Bava Batra, lays out an order: the Prophets close with the Twelve, the short books like Malachi, and the Writings close with Chronicles. So the Tanakh has more than one ending, and each one leans forward. Malachi's last lines tell the people to remember the teaching of Moses, then make a promise. In the King James words: "Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the LORD." The Prophets end with someone still on the way. At Passover, some families pour a cup for Elijah and open the door. Then a harder turn. The Talmud, in tractate Yoma, says that when the last prophets, Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi, died, the holy spirit of prophecy departed from Israel. But the same passage adds that people still heard a bat kol, an echo of a heavenly voice. Quieter, but not silence. So who carries the story now? The opening of Pirkei Avot answers with a chain. Moses received the Torah at Sinai and handed it to Joshua, Joshua to the elders, the elders to the prophets, and the prophets to the men of the Great Assembly. They gave three pieces of advice: be careful in judgment, raise up many students, and build a fence around the Torah. When the prophets go quiet, the answer is students.
screen: `MORE THAN ONE ENDING.` · then, large: `I WILL SEND YOU ELIJAH THE PROPHET.` · `PROPHECY GOES QUIET.` · `A CHAIN OF HANDS: RAISE UP STUDENTS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one ending in your own life, a graduation, a move, a funeral, a last day at a job, something that looked like the last page. Now look at the first ordinary morning after: who handed you something, or whom did you hand something to? If you pray, give thanks in words from your tradition for what continued.
Bat kol. An echo of a heavenly voice, still heard, the Talmud says, after the Tanakh closed and prophecy went quiet. Today's word.
Your line: the pages ran out; the handing-on didn't. Prophecy went quiet, and the teachers took up the chain. Day eight hundred eighty-seven, done.

howItsDone: Jews read and study the Tanakh alongside the teachings of the rabbis who came after it, and some communities study Pirkei Avot, which opens with the chain of tradition from Moses, on Sabbath afternoons in the weeks after Passover.

chat.says: When the prophets stopped, did Judaism think God's voice and teaching just went silent?
options: Not silent: a bat kol was still heard, and teachers carried the chain.
Yes, after Malachi there was no word from God and no teaching at all.
No, new prophets kept writing books that were added to the Tanakh.
chat.meaning: The Talmud says prophecy departed but a bat kol was still heard, and Pirkei Avot traces a chain of teachers who raised up many students.
